newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Sing Tao to return to black - chairman.
newsitem.headline: Sing Tao to return to black - chairman.

text.p: Sing Tao Holdings Ltd is expected to return to the black this fiscal year after the group decided to close down its loss-making evening newspaper, chairman and managing director Sally Aw said on Tuesday.
"We closed down the evening paper and that would actually help the company to cut down losses," Aw told reporters, adding that the group would save nearly HK$50 million a year from the closure.
Sing Tao Holdings would return to profit this fiscal year, she said. Sing Tao expected to announce interim results on December 27.
The group posted a loss of HK$146.42 million for the year ended March 31, 1996, on lower advertising revenues and higher newsprint costs.
Net profit was HK$286.20 million in the previous year.
Aw said the group would concentrate on the development of its Sing Tao Daily after printing the last edition of the 48-year-old evening newspaper on Tuesday.
The difficult economic situation in Hong Kong dampened advertising revenues in 1995 and early this year but Sing Tao Daily started to see a recovery from July, Aw said.
"It posted double digit growth," a Sing Tao executive said, referring to advertising revenue.
Aw said circulation also had increased but she declined to disclose the figure.
The group's English-language Hong Kong Standard was breaking even after a reorganisation, she said, while its indirectly controlled Tin Tin Daily News was making money.
Aw said while she felt sorry about the closure of the Sing Tao Evening Post, the company had to face reality.

"We have already been trying our best to improve the quality of the paper. It doesn't help because the evening public to my regret is not increasing but decreasing, so that is why we decided to close it," she said.
Aw said the major reasons for the closure were the lack of advertising and low circulation, which failed to reach targets despite a reorganisation six months ago.
"It has nothing to do with the price war," she said.
A number of major local Chinese newspapers cut prices last December in a fight for market share. Costs were rising at the same time, putting the pinch on profit margins.
But the group's two main newspapers, Sing Tao Daily and Sing Tao Evening Post, each maintained their HK$5.00 newsstand price.
Media analysts said the closure would have a positive impact on the Sing Tao group by helping to cut losses.
"It is a good decision made by Sing Tao," an analyst said, adding that the impact would show up in the second half of the next fiscal year.
"The market for evening newspapers is shrinking as most of the news in an evening newspaper is also covered by TV, radio and other media," he said.
Most of the 300 staff at the evening newspaper would be laid off, Aw said. Sixty-seven editorial jobs were terminated on Tuesday.
A Sing Tao executive said he expected severance payments would amount to about HK$10 million.
Trading in Sing Tao shares was suspended at mid-morning on Tuesday and was expected to resume on Wednesday. The share was down HK$0.075 at HK$3.525 when trading was suspended.
